clue.text: Giddy guy finds first sound of freedom leads to the gallows

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the word finds
sound of means we want a word that is pronounced like a synonym for freedom, though spelt differently

parts.note: freedom means liberty
a gibbet is a gallows on which bodies were hung

explanation.surface: A frivolous man discovers that his first taste of liberty ends on the scaffold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finds first' gives F; 'sound of' asks for LIBBERTI, which is said like LIBERTY. 'leads to' is only a link before the gallows.
explanation.definitionFit: A flibbertigibbet is a flighty, frivolous, scatterbrained person, so a giddy guy fits.

clue.text: We organised a raid to intercept weapon

indicators.note: to intercept means one piece cuts into and sits in the middle of the other

parts.note: a gun is a weapon

indicators.note: organised means the letters of a raid are put into a new order

explanation.surface: We planned a raid in order to seize an enemy weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' signals the anagram and 'to intercept' the insertion. The newspaper speaks of itself as 'we', and this puzzle appeared in that paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guardian newspaper, where this puzzle appeared, refers to itself in editorials with the first-person plural pronoun.

clue.text: I have orders to put 'vehicle first' then 'first vehicle'

indicators.note: vehicle first means take just the opening letter of the word vehicle

parts.note: first is the number one, the Roman numeral I
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone instructed to rearrange a sign reading 'vehicle first' into 'first vehicle'.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrases look like word-order instructions; really 'vehicle first' gives V, and 'first vehicle' gives I (one) and CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman has taken holy orders, so a vicar can say he has orders.

clue.text: Poet and painter and soldier and rescuer from Terror

parts.note: William Blake was both a poet and a painter
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: A list of a man's accomplishments: poet, painter, soldier and saviour from the Terror.
explanation.walkthrough: The list seems to describe one man; really Blake is poet and painter, Ney the soldier, and the whole is Sir Percy Blakeney, the Scarlet Pimpernel of Baroness Orczy's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Percy Blakeney, the Scarlet Pimpernel, smuggled aristocrats out of revolutionary France during the Reign of Terror.

clue.text: Classical scene of Apollo topping brothers

indicators.note: topping means cutting off the top, the first letter of the word

parts.note: adelphi is the Greek for brothers, as in London's Adelphi, named after the Adam brothers

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek site where the god's cult outshone a pair of siblings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topping' looks like 'surpassing' but means beheading: ADELPHI loses its A.
explanation.definitionFit: Delphi in ancient Greece was the site of the oracle and great temple of the god Apollo.

clue.text: Agreeable c-cargo distributed without noise

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the anagram goes around the other piece
distributed means the letters of c-cargo are spread about in a new order

parts.note: din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A stammered word about cargo being shared out quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distributed' signals the anagram; 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: According can mean agreeing or in harmony, an adjectival sense close to agreeable.

clue.text: Stick to this time and place

parts.note: AD, anno domini, marks years of the present era
here means this place

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep to the present moment and location.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to stick fast or keep firmly to something.

clue.text: Boy composer's kin revealed by primate

indicators.note: revealed suggests the letters are opened out and rearranged to show what they really are

parts.note: the possessive s stays in the letters here

explanation.surface: A young musician's relatives are exposed by an ape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revealed' rearranges all fifteen letters of BOY COMPOSERS KIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The proboscis monkey of Borneo, with its long nose, is a primate.

clue.text: Ancient prize encircles one cummings, writer of …

indicators.note: encircles means the first piece goes right round the second

parts.note: a laurel wreath was the prize at ancient Greek games
one is the Roman numeral I
the American poet e e cummings wrote his initials in lower case

explanation.surface: A classical wreath around a single poet, introducing a book that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encircles' puts I inside LAUREL, splitting it LAUR-I-EL. The ellipsis carries on to the next clue, which names his book.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurie Lee was the English writer of the memoir named in the following clue.

clue.text: … his weird erotic fantasy

indicators.note: fantasy suggests the letters of the preceding words are reimagined into a new shape

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, a suggestion that the writer's book was a strange sexual daydream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fantasy' rearranges HIS WEIRD EROTIC. Cider with Rosie is Laurie Lee's memoir of a Cotswold childhood, whose famous scene of a first kiss gives the surface its wink.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurie Lee's book of his Gloucestershire childhood includes an innocent erotic episode under a hay wagon.

clue.text: Democrat retaining right ways to circumvent order to dance in 19th century poems

indicators.note: retaining means the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: Barack Obama is a Democrat

indicators.note: to circumvent means to go around, so the roads surround what follows

parts.note: roads are ways
the OM is the Order of Merit
a ball is a dance

explanation.surface: A Democratic politician keeps to the right while finding routes around a summons to dance, all within Victorian verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retaining' and 'to circumvent' each signal one piece going inside another. Kipling's collection appeared in 1892; 'order' is the Order of Merit, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrack-Room Ballads is Rudyard Kipling's 1892 collection of poems about soldiers' lives.

clue.text: Saying 'pub gutted' when traveller comes in

indicators.note: comes in means the traveller is placed inside the remaining letters
gutted means the insides of the word pub are removed, leaving only its ends

parts.note: a rover is a wanderer or traveller

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the pub was wrecked when a wanderer walked in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' empties the pub of its middle letter, and 'comes in' signals the insertion; 'when' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverb is a short traditional saying expressing a general truth.

clue.text: Death to the poll

definitions.meaning: a departure from life, as an actor's departure from the stage
the word that comes before poll in the name of the survey taken as voters leave polling stations

explanation.definitionFit: Exit means a departure, including from life, and an exit poll surveys voters after voting.

clue.text: International organization to sort head for cruelty

parts.note: the UN is the United Nations
kind means sort
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbouring capes

explanation.surface: A global body sets out to sort out who heads the cruelty enquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: Unkindness is lack of kindness, a milder synonym for cruelty.

clue.text: Poet keeps sort of control on learner bit by bit

indicators.note: keeps means the poet holds the following pieces inside

parts.note: Thomas Gray wrote the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
dual control is the arrangement in a driving-school car
L is the learner plate on a British car

explanation.surface: A poet takes charge of a learner driver in stages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' signals the insertion. Learner drivers in Britain display an L plate, and instructors' cars have dual controls.
explanation.definitionFit: Gradually means by degrees, little by little, bit by bit.

clue.text: Coloured light for final cargo item

parts.note: tint means coloured, as a verb
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: Colourful lighting for the last thing loaded in a ship's hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The word break moves in the answer. John Masefield's poem Cargoes ends its list of a British coaster's freight with 'cheap tin trays'.
explanation.definitionFit: The last line of Masefield's poem Cargoes lists cheap tin trays as the final freight item.

clue.text: Subcontinental Pacific resort hosting some UK folk

indicators.note: hosting means the resort holds the other piece inside

parts.note: Bali is an Indonesian island resort on the edge of the Pacific region
ENG is short for English, some of the people of the UK

explanation.surface: An island holiday spot welcomes a few British visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hosting' signals the insertion; 'some UK folk' points to the English rather than to a whole nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Bengali people and their language come from Bengal on the Indian subcontinent.

clue.text: Fail with vision (sound) — I'm devastated

parts.note: to bomb is to fail badly

indicators.note: the bracketed sound means take a word pronounced like the synonym for vision

parts.note: sight means vision

explanation.surface: A failure of eyesight leaves the speaker crushed.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'sound' turns SIGHT into SITE. The answer speaks for itself as a ruined place.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb site is a place devastated by bombing, here speaking in the first person.

clue.text: A job, say, changed with change of views?

parts.note: a post is a job

indicators.note: changed means the letters of the word say are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether taking a new job brings a shift in opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges only the last word; 'with' is just a link to the definition, whose question mark hints at the pun on change.
explanation.definitionFit: Apostasy is the abandonment of a belief or principle, a radical change of views.

clue.text: Ranked first by setter, name entered for Lady Bracknell, say

indicators.note: entered means the abbreviation for name is put inside the other letters

parts.note: graded means ranked
A means first, as in A1
the setter refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: A rating announced by the compiler, with a name written in for a famous stage role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entered' signals the insertion. Lady Bracknell is the formidable aunt in Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Bracknell is the archetypal formidable, dignified elderly woman, an example of the type.

clue.text: To be a neighbour is about fifty-fifty — or forty-nine forty-nine?

indicators.note: is about means the first piece surrounds the second

parts.note: to abut is to border on, be a neighbour to
L is the Roman numeral fifty, so two of them give LL

explanation.surface: A neighbourly arrangement split evenly, or very nearly evenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is about' signals the insertion. Forty-nine is all but fifty, so the playful definition fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Forty-nine is almost fifty, and all but means almost, so the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: This way round is to say isn't mine

indicators.note: round means the first piece goes around the second

parts.note: this clue runs down the grid, so this way means down

explanation.surface: Turning things about to deny something belongs to you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This way round' seems an instruction to reverse; in fact 'This way' is the clue's own direction in the grid, and 'round' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To disown something is to deny any connection with it or ownership of it.

clue.text: See 11
To tie the knot is indeed old-fashioned

definitions.meaning: an archaic oath meaning indeed or forsooth, originally by Mary

explanation.definitionFit: To marry is to wed, and marry was an old interjection meaning indeed.

clue.text: See 11
Greek role insane? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: read as role in sane, PART goes inside SANE

explanation.surface: A question whether an actor's part is mad, then a hedging reply.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'insane' as 'in sane': PART goes inside SANE, and 'Not quite' drops the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spartan was a citizen of Sparta in ancient Greece.

clue.text: Just as in railroad

indicators.note: in means the first piece is placed inside the second

parts.note: an El is an elevated railroad, as in Chicago
qua is Latin for as, in the capacity of

explanation.surface: Likewise on the railways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the insertion. The El is the elevated railroad of American cities, and Latin qua means 'in the capacity of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Just and equal both mean fair or even-handed.
